clue.text: Tros Anchisiade

parts.note: surface reading: 'Trojan son of Anchises', a bare form of address; setter's reading: the Sibyl's greeting to Aeneas in Aeneid 6 pairs this with a further vocative phrase praising his divine descent

explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes half of a greeting from Aeneid 6.125-6, and the answer is the words that stand beside it in the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases address Aeneas: his father Anchises was Trojan and his mother Venus a goddess, so he is offspring of heavenly stock.

explanation.surface: A line of Virgil describing the throng of the dead pouring down to the riverbank of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap takes RIPAS; the bracketed instruction (reversed) means it is entered back to front, as SAPIR.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Aeneid the dead souls crowd to the banks of the Styx, and the Latin for banks fills the gap.

clue.text: A meaningless palindrome, suggesting the name Titus Optimus

explanation.surface: A bit of nonsense that happens to hint at an imaginary Roman.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a filler light: T is the standard abbreviation of the praenomen Titus, and the string is built symmetrically round O for Optimus.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter admits the letters mean nothing; they only read identically forwards and backwards while recalling Roman initials.

explanation.definitionFit: Aconite is the poisonous plant monkshood, which Virgil says never deceives Italian gatherers of herbs.

clue.text: Let him take (one letter missing)

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase translates as CAPIAT; 'one letter missing' drops its final T.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin uses the subjunctive mood for a third-person command, so capiat renders the English jussive phrase.

explanation.definitionFit: Cicadas are the shrill insects whose chirring fills Mediterranean trees in the midday heat, so the orchards resound with them.

clue.text: Clamorque virum stridorque ——

explanation.walkthrough: The gap needs a genitive plural to match 'virum', the shrieking 'of the ropes'.

clue.text: Et ventis et fulminis —— alis (first three letters only)

clue.text: Tyrrhenusque tubae —— per aethera clangor (first three letters only)

explanation.definitionFit: Mugire is the Latin verb for the lowing of cattle, used of the trumpet's roar.

clue.text: An imaginary proverb (two words) analogous to "pearls before swine"

explanation.walkthrough: The two words mean 'honey to a whale': cetus is a whale or sea monster, in the dative, and mel is honey.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving a sweet delicacy to a vast sea beast is as pointless as casting precious jewels to hogs.

clue.text: Tum se ad Cairtae —— fert litore portum (vowels omitted)

explanation.definitionFit: The Roman as was split into twelve unciae, and the bes was the eight-ounce share, one coin less a third.

explanation.surface: A grammar exercise on a Greek colony in the toe of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Thurii, in Calabria, was settled by Athenians close to destroyed Sybaris; Augustus was nicknamed Thurinus.

clue.text: Long

parts.note: surface reading: the English adjective for great length; setter's reading: the adverb 'for a long time', to be put into Latin

explanation.walkthrough: As throughout this puzzle, the English is to be rendered in Latin, and 'long' is read as the adverb of time, not of size.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin adverb diu means for a lengthy while, as in 'he waited long'.

explanation.definitionFit: The Latin for bronze or copper stands for a brass instrument by metonymy, naming a thing by its substance.

explanation.definitionFit: Utro asks which way, the Latin counterpart of the English question about direction.

definitions.meaning: surface reading: someone taught by great Atlas plays a golden lyre

explanation.surface: Entertainment at Dido's banquet: a minstrel singing to a gilded lyre.
explanation.walkthrough: The words mean 'long-haired Iopas', Dido's court singer, who sings of the stars as Atlas taught him.
explanation.definitionFit: Crinitus means long-haired, the traditional look of a bard modelled on Apollo, and Iopas is the singer's name.

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a string from which a place name can be guessed

definitions.text: famous for its statue of Venus
definitions.meaning: setter's reading: the Greek city of Praxiteles' Aphrodite, whose name contains all four entered letters

explanation.surface: A hint at a city celebrated for a goddess's statue.
explanation.walkthrough: The city is Cnidus, home of Praxiteles' Aphrodite of Knidos; the entry is four of its letters, C, D, N and U, as crossings dictate.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters are drawn from that Carian city's name, so they bring it to mind without spelling it.

clue.text: —— Unde Atii duxere Latini (reversed and middle consonant omitted)

indicators.note: the bracketed instruction says the shortened Latin word is entered back to front
the instruction also drops the central consonant of the Latin word

parts.note: Aeneid 5.568, 'alter Atys, genus unde Atii duxere Latini': the second Atys, from whom the Latin Atii drew their descent; the gap is genus, race

explanation.surface: Virgil flatters the Atii, Augustus's mother's family, by tracing their line to a Trojan boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle consonant omitted' takes N from GENUS, leaving GEUS, and 'reversed' gives SUEG.
explanation.definitionFit: Genus is Latin for race or stock, the lineage the Atii claimed.

explanation.definitionFit: Celemna was a small town of Campania, named among the lands of Turnus's allies.

clue.text: Haud equidem pretio inductus pulchroque juvenco venissem nec dona ——

definitions.text: Haud equidem pretio inductus pulchroque juvenco venissem
definitions.meaning: surface reading: a speaker insists no prize or fine bullock would have tempted him
setter's reading: the verb completing 'nor do I care about gifts'

explanation.surface: A proud contestant declaring he did not come for the prizes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nec moror' is a Latin idiom, literally 'nor do I delay over', meaning 'I care nothing for'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moror means I linger, and with a negative it becomes 'I set no store by', dismissing the gifts.

definitions.text: consequitur pennis sublimem in nube columbam
definitions.meaning: surface reading: something overtakes a dove high in the clouds

explanation.surface: A bird of prey stooping from a crag on a fleeing dove.
explanation.walkthrough: Virgil compares Camilla catching the fleeing Ligurian to a hawk taking a dove.
explanation.definitionFit: Accipiter is the Latin for hawk, a bird sacred to Mars and so called 'sacer ales'.

clue.text: Sed cadat ante —— mediaque inhumatus arena (reversed and last letter omitted)

definitions.text: Sed cadat ante —— mediaque inhumatus arena

indicators.note: the bracketed instruction says the shortened Latin word is entered back to front
the instruction also drops the final letter of the Latin word

parts.note: Aeneid 4.620, 'sed cadat ante diem mediaque inhumatus harena': but let him fall before his day and lie unburied on the sand; the gap is diem, day

explanation.surface: Dido curses Aeneas: may he die before his time and lie unburied in the sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last letter omitted' leaves DIE, and 'reversed' gives EID.
explanation.definitionFit: Ante diem, before the day, means an untimely death; dies is Latin for day.

clue.text: hoc —— velit et magno mercentur Atridae (reversed)

definitions.text: hoc —— velit et magno mercentur Atridae

indicators.note: the setter's bracketed instruction to write the missing Latin word backwards in the grid

parts.words: hoc —— velit et magno mercentur Atridae
parts.note: Aeneid 2.104: Sinon taunts the Trojans that killing him is what Ulysses would wish and the sons of Atreus pay dearly for

explanation.surface: The lying Greek Sinon goading his Trojan captors.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is ITHACUS, 'the Ithacan', meaning Ulysses, which goes in backwards. The Atridae are Agamemnon and Menelaus.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses ruled the island of Ithaca, so Virgil names him by his homeland as Sinon's supposed enemy.

clue.text: Suspensi Eurypylum scitantem oracula Phoebi —— (last letter omitted)

indicators.note: the bracketed instruction drops the final letter of the Latin word that fills the gap

parts.note: Aeneid 2.114, 'suspensi Eurypylum scitantem oracula Phoebi mittimus': in suspense we send Eurypylus to consult Apollo's oracle; the gap is mittimus, we send

explanation.surface: The anxious Greeks dispatch Eurypylus to ask Apollo's oracle about sailing home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last letter omitted' drops the S of MITTIMUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Mittimus is the first-person plural of mittere, to send.

clue.text: Serpitque per agmina ——

definitions.meaning: surface reading: something snakes its way through the ranks
setter's reading: Aeneid 12.239, the low noise of discontent spreading through the army

explanation.surface: Unrest creeping through the lines of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word is spelt exactly like its English descendant.
explanation.definitionFit: Murmur means a low rumbling sound of voices, the grumbling that creeps through the soldiers.

indicators.note: the bracketed instruction says the shortened Latin word is entered back to front
the instruction also drops the closing two letters of the Latin word

parts.note: Aeneid 5.560-1, 'tres equitum numero turmae, ternique vagantur ductores': three troops of horsemen and three leaders ride about; the gap is ternique, and three each

explanation.surface: The boys' cavalry display at the funeral games: three squadrons, each with its leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last two letters missing' leaves TERNIQ, and 'reversed' gives QINRET.
explanation.definitionFit: Terni is the Latin distributive for three apiece, with -que for 'and'.

clue.text: —— vel molli melius feret esseda collo (last two letters missing)

explanation.surface: A well-trained horse will pull a Gaulish war-chariot all the better with a supple neck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last two letters missing' cuts CA from BELGICA.
explanation.definitionFit: The essedum was a war-chariot of the Belgae of northern Gaul, hence Belgic.

explanation.definitionFit: Lentus means slow or tough, describing calm water that resists the oars as the wind drops.
